## Version and installation

This guide targets the revised **development version 2.0.0** of orthoDr.
CRAN currently distributes 0.6.8; its results can differ from this guide.
The numerical changes are described in the
[development release notes](https://github.com/teazrq/orthoDr/blob/master/NEWS.md).

Install the development package in your usual R user library:

```r
install.packages("remotes") # once, if needed
remotes::install_github("teazrq/orthoDr")
```

To use the CRAN release instead, run `install.packages("orthoDr")` and
consult the [CRAN reference manual](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/orthoDr/refman/orthoDr.html).

The code below is also available as a downloadable R script. In an installed
package, find it with `system.file("examples", "getting-started.R", package = "orthoDr")`.
Outputs were generated by running that script. The package checks execute
the same examples. Last digits and convergence counts can vary by platform.


``` r
library(orthoDr)
packageVersion("orthoDr")
#> [1] '2.0.0'
```

## Fit a regression model and predict

Supply an $n \times p$ numeric feature matrix and a length-$n$ outcome vector.
Here the response depends mainly on the first feature. `ndr = 1` asks for
one reduced direction. Set `keep.data = TRUE` when you will call `predict()`.
These examples use one CPU thread and an explicit iteration budget.


``` r
set.seed(101)
x_reg <- matrix(rnorm(120 * 4), ncol = 4)
y_reg <- x_reg[, 1] + 0.2 * x_reg[, 2] + rnorm(120, sd = 0.3)
new_x <- matrix(rnorm(5 * 4), ncol = 4)

reg_fit <- orthoDr_reg(
  x_reg, y_reg, method = "sir", ndr = 1,
  keep.data = TRUE, maxitr = 200, ncore = 1
)
reg_prediction <- predict(reg_fit, new_x)
dim(reg_fit$B)
#> [1] 4 1
round(reg_prediction$pred, 3)
#> [1] -0.617 -0.836 -0.172 -0.650 -0.312
reg_fit$converge
#> [1] TRUE
```

`B` has four rows and one column. `pred` contains one predicted response
for each of the five new rows. The sign of a direction is arbitrary;
compare subspaces or predictions instead of comparing signed coefficients.
`converge` reports whether the optimizer reached a stopping criterion.
If it is `FALSE`, inspect the fit and iteration budget before interpreting it.

## Fit a survival model and predict curves

Observed time is the minimum of event and censoring times. An event
indicator of **1 means an event**, and 0 means censoring. We use the
martingale estimating equation, `method = "dm"`.


``` r
set.seed(102)
x_surv <- matrix(rnorm(120 * 4), ncol = 4)
event_time <- rexp(120, rate = exp(x_surv[, 1]))
censor_time <- rexp(120, rate = 0.3)
observed_time <- pmin(event_time, censor_time)
event <- as.integer(event_time <= censor_time)
new_surv_x <- matrix(rnorm(5 * 4), ncol = 4)

surv_fit <- orthoDr_surv(
  x_surv, observed_time, event, method = "dm", ndr = 1,
  keep.data = TRUE, maxitr = 200, ncore = 1
)
surv_prediction <- predict(surv_fit, new_surv_x)
dim(surv_prediction$surv)
#> [1] 91  5
head(surv_prediction$timepoints)
#> [1] 0.001435511 0.002411730 0.003128249 0.013880143 0.013921950 0.016101402
range(surv_prediction$surv)
#> [1] 6.004596e-24 1.000000e+00
surv_fit$converge
#> [1] TRUE
```

The survival matrix has one column per new subject and one row per observed
event. `timepoints` gives those row times. Probabilities lie between 0 and 1
and decrease or stay constant over time. In the revised package, tied events
share a time label and the same post-event probability.

For a 2D plot of the fitted direction, use
`view_dr_surv(x_surv, observed_time, event, surv_fit$B, FUN = log, type = "2D")`.
The transformation argument is `FUN`, not `scale`. Use `FUN = identity`
to leave time unchanged, including when you already transformed it.
The full survival example also demonstrates 3D plots and the SKCM data.

## Learn a personalized dose and predict

This simulated reward is largest near dose $1 + 0.3 x_2$. Both the
direct and pseudo-direct methods use an explicit 12-point candidate grid.
Rewards in this example are positive. Predictions are doses in the same
units as the observed training doses.


``` r
set.seed(113)
x_dose <- matrix(runif(150 * 3, -1, 1), ncol = 3)
observed_dose <- runif(150, 0, 2)
target_dose <- 1 + 0.3 * x_dose[, 2]
reward <- 4 + x_dose[, 1] - (observed_dose - target_dose)^2 +
  rnorm(150, sd = 0.1)
new_dose_x <- x_dose[1:5, , drop = FALSE]

dose_fit <- orthoDr_pdose(
  x_dose, observed_dose, reward, method = "direct", ndr = 1,
  K = 12, lambda = 0.1, keep.data = TRUE, maxitr = 500, ncore = 1
)
dose_prediction <- predict(dose_fit, new_dose_x)
round(dose_prediction$pred, 3)
#>       [,1]
#> [1,] 1.068
#> [2,] 1.268
#> [3,] 0.863
#> [4,] 0.855
#> [5,] 1.067
dose_fit$converge
#> [1] TRUE

pseudo_fit <- orthoDr_pdose(
  x_dose, observed_dose, reward, method = "pseudo_direct", ndr = 1,
  K = 12, lambda = 0.1, keep.data = TRUE, maxitr = 150, ncore = 1
)
pseudo_prediction <- predict(pseudo_fit, new_dose_x)
round(pseudo_prediction$pred, 3)
#>       [,1]
#> [1,] 1.096
#> [2,] 1.081
#> [3,] 0.914
#> [4,] 0.899
#> [5,] 1.029
pseudo_fit$converge
#> [1] TRUE
```

Each call returns five numeric dose predictions. The two methods need not
give identical answers. The direct method's gradient stopping criterion
holds its current policy coefficients fixed; `converge = TRUE` does not
establish a globally optimal dose rule.

## Use the general optimizer

Maximize $b^T A b$ subject to $b^T b = 1$, where $A = X^T X$.
This finds the first principal component of centered $X$. We provide the
analytic gradient $2 A b$ and compare the fitted subspace with `prcomp()`.


``` r
set.seed(104)
x_pca <- scale(matrix(rnorm(100 * 6), ncol = 6), scale = FALSE)
a_pca <- crossprod(x_pca)
b_initial <- matrix(rep(1 / sqrt(6), 6), ncol = 1)
objective <- function(b, a) drop(crossprod(b, a %*% b))
gradient <- function(b, a) 2 * a %*% b

optim_fit <- ortho_optim(
  b_initial, objective, gradient, a = a_pca,
  maximize = TRUE, maxitr = 500
)
pca_direction <- prcomp(x_pca)$rotation[, 1, drop = FALSE]
pca_distance <- distance(optim_fit$B, pca_direction, type = "dist")
round(pca_distance, 6)
#> [1] 0
round(drop(crossprod(optim_fit$B)), 6)
#> [1] 1
optim_fit$converge
#> [1] TRUE
```

A subspace distance near zero indicates agreement with `prcomp()`.
The squared length of the fitted direction should be 1.
If you omit `gradient`, the solver approximates it numerically.

## Reference and reproducibility

Use `help("orthoDr_reg")`, `help("orthoDr_surv")`, `help("orthoDr_pdose")`,
`help("predict.orthoDr")`, and `help("ortho_optim")` for your installed
version's argument and return-value documentation.

The guide and downloadable scripts are maintained together under
[`inst/examples`](https://github.com/teazrq/orthoDr/tree/master/inst/examples).
The package's `tests/examples.R` executes these examples during `R CMD check`.
Maintainers can regenerate this guide with
`Rscript tools/build-getting-started.R` using a shared installation of knitr.
